learning_objective: 🎯 Take vectors into the 3D world to find the equations of flying lines and calculate the shortest distance between intersecting paths in space!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Direction cosines (l, m, n) are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the x, y, and z axes. Direction ratios (a, b, c) are just any numbers proportional to those cosines.
To define a straight line in 3D space, you only need two things: a starting point (a position vector) and a direction to travel in (a parallel vector).
In 2D, lines either intersect or are parallel. But in 3D, two lines can pass by each other like airplanes at different altitudes—never intersecting, yet not parallel. These are called Skew Lines!
Even though skew lines never touch, there is one specific spot where they get closest to each other. We use a powerful formula involving dot and cross products to find this exact distance.

fun_activity.title: 💡 The Room Corner Origin
fun_activity.instructions: Look at the bottom corner of your room. That is (0,0,0). The floor edges are the X and Y axes, and the wall corner going up is the Z axis. Imagine a laser pointer beam shooting across the room—that's a 3D line!

exam_tips: 📌 Always know how to convert seamlessly between the Vector equation of a line ($\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \vec{b}$) and the Cartesian equation ($(x-x_1)/a = (y-y_1)/b = (z-z_1)/c$).
📌 The relationship $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$ is a golden rule for direction cosines. (Note: Direction ratios $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$ do NOT equal 1).
📌 Memorize the Shortest Distance between Skew Lines formula. It is heavily tested and usually a guaranteed 3 or 4-mark question.
quick_recap: ⭐ You need a point and a direction to form a line in 3D.
⭐ Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting.
⭐ Direction cosines are unique, but a line has infinite direction ratios.
